Getting Started¶

Getting Spack is easy.
You can clone it from the GitHub repository using this command:

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git

$

=

2

This will create a directory called spack.
Once you have cloned Spack, we recommend sourcing the appropriate script for your shell.

spack

For bash, zsh and sh users:

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh

$

For csh and tcsh users:

$ source spack/share/spack/setup-env.csh

$ source spack/share/spack/setup-env.csh

$

source

For fish users:

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.fish

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.fish

$

Now you’re ready to use Spack!

List packages you can install¶

Once Spack is ready, you can list all the packages it knows about with the following command:

$ spack list

$ spack list

$

If you want to get more information on a specific package, for instance hdf5, you can use:

hdf5

$ spack info hdf5

$ spack info hdf5

$

hdf5

This command shows information about hdf5, including a brief description, the versions of the package Spack knows about, and all the options you can activate when installing.

hdf5

As you can see, it’s quite simple to gather basic information on packages before you install them!

The first command you run with Spack may take a while, as Spack builds caches to speed up future commands.

Installing your first package¶

To install most packages, Spack needs a compiler suite to be available.
To search your machine for available compilers, you can run:

$ spack compiler find

$ spack compiler find

$

The command shows users whether any compilers were found and where their configuration is stored.
If the search was successful, you can now list known compilers, and get an output similar to the following:

Spack¶

Spack is a package management tool designed to support multiple versions and configurations of software on a wide variety of platforms and environments.
It was designed for large supercomputing centers, where many users and application teams share common installations of software on clusters with exotic architectures, using libraries that do not have a standard ABI.
Spack is non-destructive: installing a new version does not break existing installations, so many configurations can coexist on the same system.

Most importantly, Spack is simple.
It offers a simple spec syntax so that users can specify versions and configuration options concisely.
Spack is also simple for package authors: package files are written in pure Python, and specs allow package authors to maintain a single file for many different builds of the same package.

See the Feature Overview for examples and highlights.

Feature Overview

Get Spack from the GitHub repository and install your first package:

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git
$ cd spack/bin
$ ./spack install libelf

chunks.content:
Spack

Spack is a package management tool designed to support multiple
versions and configurations of software on a wide variety of platforms
and environments.  It was designed for large supercomputing centers,
where many users and application teams share common installations of
software on clusters with exotic architectures, using libraries that
do not have a standard ABI.  Spack is non-destructive: installing a
new version does not break existing installations, so many
configurations can coexist on the same system.

Most importantly, Spack is simple.  It offers a simple spec syntax
so that users can specify versions and configuration options
concisely.  Spack is also simple for package authors: package files
are written in pure Python, and specs allow package authors to
maintain a single file for many different builds of the same package.

See the Feature Overview for examples and highlights.

Feature Overview

Get Spack from the GitHub repository and install your first
package:

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git
$ cd spack/bin
$ ./spack install libelf

Getting Started¶

Getting Spack is easy.
You can clone it from the GitHub repository using this command:

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git

$

=

2

This will create a directory called spack.
Once you have cloned Spack, we recommend sourcing the appropriate script for your shell.

spack

For bash, zsh and sh users:

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.sh

$

For csh and tcsh users:

$ source spack/share/spack/setup-env.csh

$ source spack/share/spack/setup-env.csh

$

source

For fish users:

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.fish

$ . spack/share/spack/setup-env.fish

$

Now you’re ready to use Spack!

List packages you can install¶

Once Spack is ready, you can list all the packages it knows about with the following command:

$ spack list

$ spack list

$

If you want to get more information on a specific package, for instance hdf5, you can use:

hdf5

$ spack info hdf5

$ spack info hdf5

$

hdf5

This command shows information about hdf5, including a brief description, the versions of the package Spack knows about, and all the options you can activate when installing.

hdf5

As you can see, it’s quite simple to gather basic information on packages before you install them!

Slowdown on the very first command
The first command you run with Spack may take a while, as Spack builds caches to speed up future commands.

# 

Installing your first package¶

To install most packages, Spack needs a compiler suite to be available.
To search your machine for available compilers, you can run:

$ spack compiler find

$ spack compiler find

$

The command shows users whether any compilers were found and where their configuration is stored.
If the search was successful, you can now list known compilers, and get an output similar to the following:

$ spack compiler list
==> Available compilers
-- gcc ubuntu20.04-x86_64 ---------------------------------------
[e]  gcc@9.4.0  [e]  gcc@8.4.0  [e]  gcc@10.5.0

$ spack compiler list
==> Available compilers
-- gcc ubuntu20.04-x86_64 ---------------------------------------

$

Install further prerequisites, see Spack Prerequisites, and repeat the search above.

Congratulations!
You just installed your first package with Spack!

Use the software you just installed¶

Once you have installed tcl, you can immediately use it by starting the tclsh with its absolute path:

tcl

tclsh

$ /home/spack/.local/spack/opt/linux-icelake/tcl-8.6.12-6vo5hxeqw5plzd6gvzm74wlfz5stnzcv/bin/tclsh

Hello world!

$ /home/spack/.local/spack/opt/linux-icelake/tcl-8.6.12-6vo5hxeqw5plzd6gvzm74wlfz5stnzcv/bin/tclsh
>% echo "Hello world!"
Hello world!

$

>% echo "Hello world!"

Hello world!

This works, but using such a long absolute path is not the most convenient way to run an executable.

The simplest way to have tclsh available on the command line is:

tclsh

$ spack load tcl

Spack¶

Spack is a package management tool designed to support multiple versions and configurations of software on a wide variety of platforms and environments.
It was designed for large supercomputing centers, where many users and application teams share common installations of software on clusters with exotic architectures, using libraries that do not have a standard ABI.
Spack is non-destructive: installing a new version does not break existing installations, so many configurations can coexist on the same system.

Most importantly, Spack is simple.
It offers a simple spec syntax so that users can specify versions and configuration options concisely.
Spack is also simple for package authors: package files are written in pure Python, and specs allow package authors to maintain a single file for many different builds of the same package.

See the Feature Overview for examples and highlights.

$ cd spack/bin
$ ./spack install libelf

chunks.content:
Spack

Spack is a package management tool designed to support multiple
versions and configurations of software on a wide variety of platforms
and environments.  It was designed for large supercomputing centers,
where many users and application teams share common installations of
software on clusters with exotic architectures, using libraries that
do not have a standard ABI.  Spack is non-destructive: installing a
new version does not break existing installations, so many
configurations can coexist on the same system.

Most importantly, Spack is simple.  It offers a simple spec syntax
so that users can specify versions and configuration options
concisely.  Spack is also simple for package authors: package files
are written in pure Python, and specs allow package authors to
maintain a single file for many different builds of the same package.

See the Feature Overview for examples and highlights.

Feature Overview

Get Spack from the GitHub repository and install your first
package:

$ git clone --depth=2 https://github.com/spack/spack.git
$ cd spack/bin
$ ./spack install libelf
